title: Vinesh Phogat Lost 4-6 to Meenakshi Goyat. The Supreme Court Has Closed the Case. Her Asian Games Dream Is Over.
excerpt: Three-time Olympian Vinesh Phogat lost in the Asian Games trials after a legal battle that went from the Delhi High Court to the Supreme Court. The court fight is over. The questions it raised are not.
body:
It took a Delhi High Court order, a Supreme Court hearing, a national debate about motherhood in sport, and weeks of legal wrangling for Vinesh Phogat to step onto the wrestling mat at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium in New Delhi. When she finally did, on May 30, the three-time Olympian lasted one match. She lost 4-6 to Meenakshi Goyat of Jind in the women's 53kg semifinal and failed to qualify for the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court closed the chapter. A bench of Justices PS Narasimha and Aravind Kumar dismissed the Wrestling Federation of India's petition challenging the High Court order that had allowed Phogat to compete, deeming it infructuous now that the trials were over. The legal machinery that had consumed Indian wrestling for weeks ground to a quiet halt.

"In view of subsequent developments, this SLP is rendered infructuous," the bench said. "This Court will not be taken as having reiterated the findings and observations of the High Court. The issues are kept open."

The Road to the Mat

Phogat's journey back to competitive wrestling began with a fight against her own federation. The WFI had introduced selection criteria requiring medal finishes at the 2025 Senior Nationals, the 2026 Federation Cup, or the Under-20 Nationals. Phogat, who had taken a sabbatical in December 2024, become a mother in July 2025, and informed the WFI she would be available from January 2026, met none of these requirements.

She also carried an unresolved anti-doping issue. The International Testing Agency had flagged a missed test in January 2026. Phogat said she had to attend the Haryana assembly as an MLA. The ITA did not accept the explanation.

The Delhi High Court cut through the bureaucratic thicket on May 22. A division bench of Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia held that the WFI's selection policy was "clearly exclusionary in nature" and that "motherhood cannot become a ground for exclusion or marginalisation of female athletes." The court ordered that Phogat be allowed to compete, with the trials to be video-recorded and conducted under independent SAI and IOA oversight.

The WFI challenged the order in the Supreme Court. On May 29, the apex court allowed Phogat to participate while expressing reservations about the High Court's approach. The direction was clear: "We are not stopping, you go and participate."

Ten Months After Giving Birth

Phogat walked onto the mat roughly ten months after giving birth. She had been training while caring for an infant, preparing for a weight category that was shifted from 50kg to 53kg after the WFI revised its initial restriction. The odds were never in her favour, and the scoreline — 4-6 to a younger, match-fit Goyat — reflected the reality of returning to elite sport on a compressed timeline.

In the press conference afterward, Phogat was defiant. "I did as well as I could have. I gave my 100 per cent. I believe that I should have no regrets once I leave the mat," she said. "I'll put in more effort and work, but I'm happy that my son will grow up and see that when he was 10 months old, his mother was training. I want to become the motivation for my child."

She also did not hold back on the WFI. "Everyone saw how fairly things happened and how many didn't. Everyone knows how much manipulation happened. The whole country knows."

What Remains

The Supreme Court's closure of the case is procedural, not substantive. The bench explicitly kept the underlying issues open, and the matter remains pending before a single-judge bench of the Delhi High Court. That ruling will likely shape how Indian sports federations frame selection eligibility for athletes returning from maternity leave — a question with implications far beyond wrestling.

For Phogat, the immediate future is uncertain. At 32, a return to the highest level of wrestling would require sustained training, cleared anti-doping obligations, and a federation willing to provide a pathway. None of those conditions currently exist.

What is not uncertain is the precedent her fight has set. The Delhi High Court's observation — that a woman's body is her own and maternity leave cannot be weaponised against female athletes — entered the legal record. Whether or not Vinesh Phogat wrestles again, that sentence will outlast every bout she has ever fought.

Sources: LiveLaw, India News Stream, Bar and Bench, Dainik Bhaskar
